facts.statement: Carnotaurus lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 69 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Carnotaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, between 69 and 66 million years ago.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus is classified as a derived member of the Abelisauridae family.
facts.quote: Carnotaurus is a derived member of the Abelisauridae, a group of large theropods that occupied the large predatorial niche in the southern landmasses of Gondwana during the late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus is often considered part of the Brachyrostra clade, a group of short-snouted theropods restricted to South America.
facts.quote: Within the Abelisauridae, the genus is often considered a member of the Brachyrostra, a clade of short-snouted forms restricted to South America.

facts.statement: The holotype skeleton of Carnotaurus was discovered in 1984 in the Chubut Province of Argentina within the La Colonia Formation.
facts.quote: The skeleton, found in 1984, was uncovered in the Chubut Province of Argentina from rocks of the La Colonia Formation.

facts.statement: The only known skeleton of Carnotaurus was unearthed in 1984 by an expedition led by paleontologist José Bonaparte.
facts.quote: The only skeleton (holotype MACN-CH 894) was unearthed in 1984 by an expedition led by Argentinian paleontologist José Bonaparte.

facts.statement: José Bonaparte described Carnotaurus sastrei as a new genus and species in 1985.
facts.quote: In 1985, Bonaparte published a note presenting Carnotaurus sastrei as a new genus and species and briefly describing the skull and lower jaw.

facts.statement: The Carnotaurus skeleton was found on the "Pocho Sastre" farm near Bajada Moreno in the Telsen Department of Chubut Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: The skeleton was collected on a farm named "Pocho Sastre" near Bajada Moreno in the Telsen Department of Chubut Province, Argentina.

facts.statement: The name Carnotaurus translates to "meat-eating bull," referencing the animal's bull-like horns.
facts.quote: The generic name Carnotaurus is derived from the Latin carno [carnis] ("flesh") and taurus ("bull") and can be translated with "meat-eating bull", an allusion to the animal's bull-like horns.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus possessed two thick horns above its eyes and a very deep skull resting on a muscular neck.
facts.quote: It had two thick horns above the eyes, a unique feature unseen in all other carnivorous dinosaurs, and a very deep skull sitting on a muscular neck.

facts.statement: Large bumps lined the sides of the Carnotaurus, interrupting the scale mosaic, and there is no evidence of feathers.
facts.quote: The mosaic was interrupted by large bumps that lined the sides of the animal, and there are no hints of feathers.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the horns and muscular neck of Carnotaurus may have been used for fighting other individuals of its species.
facts.quote: The distinctive horns and the muscular neck may have been used in fighting others of its species.

facts.statement: Studies suggest rivaling Carnotaurus individuals may have fought using quick head blows, slow skull pushes, or head-on ramming with horns acting as shock absorbers.
facts.quote: According to separate studies, rivaling individuals may have combated each other with quick head blows, by slow pushes with the upper sides of their skulls, or by ramming each other head-on, using their horns as shock absorbers.

facts.statement: The diet of Carnotaurus is debated; some studies suggest it hunted large prey like sauropods, while others indicate it preyed mainly on small animals.
facts.quote: The feeding habits of Carnotaurus remain unclear: some studies suggested the animal was able to hunt down very large prey such as sauropods, while other studies found it preyed mainly on relatively small animals.

facts.statement: The single known individual of Carnotaurus was approximately 7.5 to 8 meters long, making it one of the largest abelisaurids.
facts.quote: The only known individual was about 7.5 - 8 m in length, making Carnotaurus one of the largest abelisaurids.

facts.statement: Estimates for the mass of Carnotaurus vary across studies, ranging from 1,306 kg to 2,100 kg depending on the method used.
facts.quote: Its mass is estimated to have been 1,350 kg, 1,500 kg, 2,000 kg, 2,100 kg, and 1,306 - 1743 kg in separate studies that used different estimation methods.

facts.statement: The left femur of the known Carnotaurus individual measures 103 cm in length with an average diameter of only 11 cm.
facts.quote: The left femur (thigh bone) of the individual measures 103 cm in length, but shows an average diameter of only 11 cm.

facts.statement: The Carnotaurus skull measured 59.6 cm in length and was proportionally shorter and deeper than in other large carnivorous dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The skull, measuring 59.6 cm in length, was proportionally shorter and deeper than in any other large carnivorous dinosaur.

facts.statement: In 2020, Cerroni and colleagues argued that the keratinous sheaths on the horns were not greatly longer than the bony cores.
facts.quote: Mauricio Cerroni and colleagues, in 2020, agreed that the horns supported keratinous sheaths, but argued that these sheaths would not have been greatly longer than the bony cores.

facts.statement: The Carnotaurus had four premaxillary and twelve maxillary teeth on each side of the upper jaw and fifteen dentary teeth per side on the lower jaw.
facts.quote: On each side of the upper jaws there were four premaxillary and twelve maxillary teeth, while the lower jaws were equipped with fifteen dentary teeth per side.

facts.statement: Replacement teeth in the Carnotaurus had low, flattened crowns that were closely spaced and inclined forward at approximately 45 degrees.
facts.quote: The replacement teeth had low, flattened crowns, were closely spaced, and inclined forwards at approximately 45°.

facts.statement: The Carnotaurus neck was nearly straight and unusually wide, especially at its base, unlike the S-curve seen in other theropods.
facts.quote: The neck was nearly straight, rather than having the S-curve seen in other theropods, and also unusually wide, especially towards its base.

facts.statement: The Carnotaurus hand lacked carpalia, causing the metacarpals to articulate directly with the forearm.
facts.quote: There were no carpalia in the hand, so that the metacarpals articulated directly with the forearm.

facts.statement: A 2009 study suggests that abelisaurid arms were vestigial, with nerve fibers reduced to an extent similar to modern emus and kiwis.
facts.quote: A 2009 study suggests that the arms were vestigial in abelisaurids, because nerve fibers responsible for stimulus transmission were reduced to an extent seen in today's emus and kiwis, which also have vestigial forelimbs.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus is the first theropod dinosaur known to have significant fossil skin impressions.
facts.quote: Carnotaurus was the first theropod dinosaur discovered with a significant number of fossil skin impressions.

facts.statement: There is no evidence that Carnotaurus had feathers.
facts.quote: There is no evidence of feathers.

facts.statement: The sides and front of the Carnotaurus snout show a scaly covering possibly similar to flat scales found in modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: A hummocky surface with grooves, pits, and small openings is found on the sides and front of the snout and indicates a scaly covering, possibly with flat scales as in today's crocodilians.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests a row of large scales probably surrounded the eye of Carnotaurus.
facts.quote: A row of large scales did probably surround the eye, as indicated by a hummocky surface with longitudinal grooves on the lacrimal and postorbital bones.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus is a well-understood genus within the family Abelisauridae, which was restricted to the supercontinent Gondwana.
facts.quote: Carnotaurus is one of the best-understood genera of the Abelisauridae, a family of large theropods restricted to the ancient southern supercontinent Gondwana.

facts.statement: In 2009, Juan Canale and colleagues created the clade Brachyrostra to include Carnotaurus but exclude Majungasaurus.
facts.quote: Juan Canale and colleagues, in 2009, erected the new clade Brachyrostra to include Carnotaurus but not Majungasaurus

facts.statement: A 2024 study identified Carnotaurini as a valid clade containing Carnotaurus, Aucasaurus, Niebla, and Koleken.
facts.quote: A 2024 study recovered Carnotaurini as a valid clade consisting of Carnotaurus, Aucasaurus, Niebla and Koleken.

facts.statement: Paleontologists do not universally accept the subgroups Carnotaurinae and Carnotaurini.
facts.quote: Paleontologists do not universally accept these groups.

facts.statement: The specific function of the horns on Carnotaurus is not entirely clear.
facts.quote: The use of these horns is not entirely clear.

facts.statement: Greg Paul proposed in 1988 that the horns were used as butting weapons, noting the small eye sockets would protect the eyes during combat.
facts.quote: Greg Paul (1988) proposed that the horns were butting weapons and that the small orbita would have minimized the possibility of hurting the eyes while fighting.

facts.statement: Gerardo Mazzetta and colleagues suggested in 1998 that Carnotaurus used its horns like rams, calculating its neck could withstand head-on collisions at speeds of 5.7 m/s.
facts.quote: Gerardo Mazzetta and colleagues (1998) suggested that Carnotaurus used its horns in a way similar to rams. They calculated that the neck musculature was strong enough to absorb the force of two individuals colliding with their heads frontally at a speed of 5.7 m/s each.

facts.statement: Fernando Novas interpreted several skeletal features in 2009 as adaptations for delivering head blows.
facts.quote: Fernando Novas (2009) interpreted several skeletal features as adaptations for delivering blows with the head.

facts.statement: Rafael Delcourt suggested in 2018 that the horns could have been used for slow headbutting/shoving like marine iguanas or for striking necks/flanks like giraffes.
facts.quote: Rafael Delcourt, in 2018, suggested that the horns could have been used either in slow headbutting and shoving, as seen in the modern marine iguana, or in blows to the opponent's neck and flanks, as seen in the modern giraffe.

facts.statement: Studies published in 2021 suggest that larger feature scales on Carnotaurus were randomly distributed rather than in discrete rows as previously depicted.
facts.quote: More recent studies of the skin of Carnotaurus published in 2021 suggest that previous depictions of the scales on the body are inaccurate, and the larger feature scales were randomly distributed along the body, not distributed in discrete rows like in older artistic depictions and illustrations.

facts.statement: The variation in scale size on Carnotaurus may have helped regulate body heat due to its large size and active lifestyle.
facts.quote: This scale differentiation may have been related to regulating body heat and shedding excess heat via thermoregulation due to its large body size and active lifestyle.

facts.statement: Analyses by Mazzetta and colleagues in 1998, 2004, and 2009 suggest Carnotaurus was capable of quick but not strong bites.
facts.quote: Analyses of the jaw structure of Carnotaurus by Mazzetta and colleagues, in 1998, 2004, and 2009, suggest that the animal was capable of quick bites, but not strong ones.

facts.statement: Mazzetta and colleagues estimated Carnotaurus had a bite force of around 3,341 newtons in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, Mazzetta and colleagues estimated a bite force of around 3,341 newtons.

facts.statement: The posterior bite force of Carnotaurus was estimated at 7,172 newtons.
facts.quote: The posterior bite force at the back of the jaws meanwhile, was estimated at 7,172 newtons.

facts.statement: Cerroni and colleagues (2020) argued that Carnotaurus skull flexibility was restricted to the lower jaw with little to no skull kinesis.
facts.quote: Cerroni and colleagues, in 2020, argued that flexibility was restricted to the lower jaw, while the thickened skull roof and the ossification of several cranial joints suggest that the skull had no or only little kinesis.

facts.statement: Robert Bakker (1998) found Carnotaurus mainly fed on very large prey, especially sauropods.
facts.quote: Robert Bakker (1998) found that Carnotaurus mainly fed upon very large prey, especially sauropods.

facts.statement: Mazzetta and colleagues (1998, 1999) presumed Carnotaurus was a swift runner based on thigh bone adaptations.
facts.quote: Mazzetta and colleagues (1998, 1999) presumed that Carnotaurus was a swift runner, arguing that the thigh bone was adapted to withstand high bending moments while running.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus likely had diminished ability to make tight turns because its hip and tail had to move simultaneously.
facts.quote: As a consequence, the ability to make tight turns would have been diminished, because the hip and tail had to be turned simultaneously, unlike in other theropods.

facts.statement: The endocranial cavity volume of Carnotaurus was 168.8 cm³.
facts.quote: The volume of the endocranial cavity was 168.8 cm3, although the brain would only have filled a fraction of this space.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus had an encephalization quotient larger than Majungasaurus but smaller than tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: This results in a reptile encephalization quotient (a measure of intelligence) larger than that of the related Majungasaurus but smaller than in tyrannosaurids.

facts.statement: Carnotaurus had large olfactory bulbs and relatively small optic lobes.
facts.quote: The olfactory bulbs, which housed the sense of smell, were large, while the optic lobes, which were responsible for sight, were relatively small.

facts.statement: Cerroni and Paulina-Carabajal hypothesized Carnotaurus relied more on smell than other abelisaurids.
facts.quote: As hypothesized by Cerroni and Paulina-Carabajal, this downward-curvature, together with the large size of the bulbs, might indicate that Carnotaurus relied more on the sense of smell than other abelisaurids.

facts.statement: Hearing in Carnotaurus might have been poorly developed, indicated by a short inner ear lagena.
facts.quote: Hearing might have been poorly developed in Carnotaurus and other abelisaurids, as indicated by the short lagena of the inner ear.
